transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-15
Time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Avalon Head of ML), Priya Rao (Avalon Infra), Tom Alvarez (Avalon CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Discussed Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for Avalon use cases, focused on per-token pricing, batching and caching levers to hit $/inference budget. Action: Redwood to send pricing and run bench.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick roll call. I'm Jordan Park from Redwood.
[00:05] Ethan Cole: Hi Jordan, Ethan here.
[00:07] Priya Rao: Priya on infra.
[00:09] Tom Alvarez: Tom, CTO.
[00:11] Maya Singh: Maya from Redwood infra/SE.
[00:15] Jordan Park: Cool. Quick agenda we want to understand your current stack, traffic, latency SLAs, and obviously budget constraints around per token cost and total monthly run-rate. Is that right, Ethan?
[00:25] Ethan Cole: Yup that's right. We're evaluating running large language features across our trading support workflows — a mix of classification, summarization, and some generation for analyst notes. Main thing is cost predictability.
[00:35] Tom Alvarez: Also data controls, we need audit logs and KMS, maybe private deployment if it's needed for compliance.
[00:41] Maya Singh: Yeah we see that a lot. Quick qualifier Q: what's your current usage and what vendor are you using now?
[00:48] Ethan Cole: Currently prototyping on OpenAI, about 200k tokens/day across peak windows, bursts to ~1k qps for short times, average 3 requests/sec overall. Latency SLOs are 300–500 ms for short prompts, and we want 95th <= 800 ms for longer contexts. Budget goal is under $30k/month for inference as a first target.
[01:12] Priya Rao: We run in GCP, VPC peering is standard, and we need to keep logs for audits for 12 months.
[01:20] Jordan Park: Great. So three paths: Hosted (Redwood API), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), Private (VPC or on-prem). For per-token economics, hosted is simplest — per-token with volume tiers; dedicated gives better unit pricing once you commit, and private gives maximal control but incurs infra ops and license fees.
[01:40] Ethan Cole: Curious ballpark numbers. How do you compare to say OpenAI per token, and then how does Dedicated amortize?
[01:48] Maya Singh: Roughly speaking, hosted per-token varies by model class — open LLMs with Redwood-catalog models are typically cheaper than closed providers. For example, at your volume, you'd see X to Y cents per 1k tokens for generation models; we can get more aggressive with reserved capacity. Dedicated is more like a committed monthly at model throughput levels — you get lower cost per token because you're amortizing GPU costs.
[02:10] Ethan Cole: X to Y cents is a bit fuzzy, can you be more concrete?
[02:14] Jordan Park: We avoid exact numbers in public transcripts but in the deck we'll show ranges. Off the top: hosted gen models at your scale might be around $0.5–$1.5 per 1k tokens depending on model family and streaming vs non-streaming. With dedicated, effective unit costs can drop 30–60% depending on utilization and batching.
[02:36] Priya Rao: Ok that variance matters. Can you explain batching and caching levers we should tune to get to the lower end?
[02:42] Maya Singh: Sure. Two main levers: batching (collecting tokens from multiple requests to run in a batch on the GPU) and prefix/KV caching (if you have repeated context or system prompts). Batching increases throughput but adds latency; Redwood supports dynamic batching with policies to balance latency SLOs. KV cache reduces compute for repeated prefixes — can cut token compute significantly if you have stable prompt templates. Also model quantization (int8/int4) reduces memory and can increase throughput at very small quality tradeoffs.
[03:08] Tom Alvarez: For our analyst notes, we have stable templates and a few long-running contexts — sounds like caching could help. How much savings are typical?
[03:15] Maya Singh: It depends, but for stable prefixes you can see 20–40% CPU/GPU savings, in some cases more if most of the prompt is static. Batching depends on request shape — with 1k qps peaks we can batch across requests to get good utilization.
[03:28] Ethan Cole: We're worried about tail latency — if we batch too aggressively we'll exceed SLOs. How does Redwood control that?
[03:34] Maya Singh: We support latency-first policies: you can set a max batching delay (e.g., 5–10ms) or route latency-sensitive routes to dedicated low-latency nodes and non-critical to cheaper nodes. Also automatic fallback to smaller models for degraded capacity.
[03:47] Priya Rao: Does dedicated mean you get the whole GPU, or shared? What's isolation?
[03:51] Jordan Park: Dedicated is reserved nodes for your tenancy; processes may still multiplex but capacity is isolated for your traffic. You can choose strict isolation for compliance needs. Private gives you the control to run in your VPC or on-prem.
[04:03] Ethan Cole: What's the onboarding cost for Private? We have compliance windows — might need Private for certain datasets.
[04:09] Maya Singh: Private has an enterprise fee and infra ops either via our managed private (we provision into your cloud under a contract) or self-managed package. There's a setup lead time — typically 4–8 weeks for VPC/private depending on approvals.
[04:21] Tom Alvarez: Are there tools to estimate expected $/month given our token distro?
[04:25] Jordan Park: Yes — we'll ask you for sample prompt set and token distribution and run a benchmark estimate. We'll simulate batching patterns to estimate effective token compute and provide both hosted and dedicated cost models.
[04:36] Ethan Cole: Let's talk concrete example: suppose we have 200k tokens/day, average 30% generation, 70% embeddings/classification. What's the math?
[04:45] Maya Singh: Ok, short math: embeddings cost per unit is separate — often lower per request but depends on dimension and model. For gen tokens assume 200k * 30% = 60k gen tokens/day. Multiply by per-token rate. With batching you can reduce GPU cycles per token by say 15–40% depending on peak-to-average. We'll run the spreadsheet.
[05:05] Priya Rao: Any hidden fees? Data egress? Logging retention costs?
[05:10] Jordan Park: For hosted, data transfer costs follow cloud provider egress; Redwood's billing is per token and optional add-ons (longer observability retention). Dedicated includes the GPU and infra, private has licensing. We'll include all line items in the deck.
[05:21] Ethan Cole: Regarding security, we need SSO (SAML), RBAC, audit logs, HSM/KMS for key management and per-tenant encryption.
[05:29] Maya Singh: We support SAML, fine-grained RBAC, audit log export, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS/GCP/partner HSM). For private you can bring your own KMS keys.
[05:37] Tom Alvarez: Good. For POC, we want to run a sample 24-hour test to validate latency and costs. Can you support that?
[05:43] Jordan Park: Absolutely. Typical POC is 2–4 weeks, we do a scoped benchmark with your sample prompts. For quick pricing we can run a 24–48 hour smoke test as well.
[05:51] Ethan Cole: One concern: model drift and quality regressions when we quantize or change models. How do you monitor?
[05:58] Maya Singh: Redwood Optimize ties quality monitoring to evals and prompt sets; we can alert on regressions and automatically rollback or route to a fallback model. We also store token-level traces for debugging.
[06:09] Priya Rao: How do we think about utilization for dedicated to hit the sweet spot vs hosted? We don't want to overcommit.
[06:16] Maya Singh: We ask for usage profiles: peak qps, average qps, cost target. There's a utilization curve; dedicated only makes sense if you can get to ~60–70% GPU utilization during committed hours — otherwise hosted may be cheaper despite higher unit price. Also burst credits can cover spikes.
[06:32] Ethan Cole: If we commit to dedicated, what kind of discounting / contractual terms are typical?
[06:37] Jordan Park: Depends on term length and size; annual commitments get best pricing. We can model a 12-month commit vs month-to-month and include burst allowances. We'll put the ranges in the deck.
[06:48] Tom Alvarez: For the 1k qps peaks — that seems large — are you saying Redwood can sustain that with batching?
[06:53] Maya Singh: Yes, with autoscaling across GPU pools, smart routing, and batching you'll get high throughput. We'd size the dedicated pool to expected peak throughput and use routing policies for critical routes.
[07:02] Ethan Cole: A few quick clarifying Qs: 1) Do you expose token-level billing? 2) Can we limit model families per environment? 3) How fast are rollouts?
[07:10] Jordan Park: 1) Yes token-level cost and per-route breakdown in the console. 2) Yes, you can pin models per route/environment. 3) Rollouts can be canary/A-B and we support automatic fallback.
[07:19] Priya Rao: For data retention we need 12-month logs; what's the price impact?
[07:24] Maya Singh: Observability retention is an add-on; we'll quantify in the deck.
[07:29] Ethan Cole: On the technical bench, what's the difference between quantization at int8 vs int4 impacts on latency and quality?
[07:36] Maya Singh: int8 is usually safe with small quality drop, int4 gives bigger gains but may need model-specific evaluation. We can recommend profiles based on your models and run QA.
[07:46] Tom Alvarez: Any examples of customers in finance?
[07:49] Jordan Park: We work with several mid-market finance orgs; happy to connect references under NDA.
[07:54] Ethan Cole: Sounds good. Let's talk about next steps — POC and pricing.
[07:59] Jordan Park: We'll deliver: pricing deck, SOC2/security package, and a bench plan. Maya will draft recommended batching/cache settings and quantization profiles. Does that timeline work?
[08:09] Priya Rao: Yes, seems good. Also we'll share sample prompts and token distribution.
[08:13] Ethan Cole: One more micro thing — how do you handle embeddings cost? We use high-volume embeddings for semantic search.
[08:19] Maya Singh: Embeddings endpoints are metered separately; there are multi-embedding and batching techniques there too. We can suggest model families that give best cost-quality tradeoff for search.
[08:28] Jordan Park: Ok last piece, any blockers for getting a POC started?
[08:31] Tom Alvarez: Approvals for data egress and legal signoff, but we'll try to expedite.
[08:36] Jordan Park: Great. I'll recap action items at the end.
[08:39] ---interruption/crosstalk---
[08:42] Maya Singh: Quick technical note: when we say batch delay we mean the additional ms — we can set per-route SLO to tune. Also KV cache sometimes gets transcribed as K V cash, sorry — transcription error.
[08:55] Ethan Cole: Ha, noted.
[09:00] Jordan Park: Recap: 1) Redwood to send pricing deck with hosted/dedicated/private line items and estimated unit economics; 2) SOC2 and KMS docs; 3) Maya to propose batching/caching/quantization configs; 4) Avalon to share prompt samples and throughput targets; 5) Schedule POC scoping for week of 2026-12-22.
[09:25] Priya Rao: Agreed.
[09:28] Ethan Cole: Good meeting, thanks folks.
[09:31] Jordan Park: Thanks everyone.
[09:35] End of call.
